page.title: Creative Operations for Startups: First Decisions
page.description: Learn the first decisions to make when setting up creative operations for a startup, including workflow stages, tool choices, and team structure.
page.h1: What should you decide first about creative operations for startups?
page.definition: Creative operations for startups is the system that moves ideas from brief to published asset without chaos. It defines intake, review, approval, and publishing steps so a small team can ship consistent work fast.
page.quick_answer: Map the seven stages from intake to reporting, assign one owner per stage, and pick one tool for work management before you hire.

sections.h2: Which workflow stages do you need from day one?

blocks.p: Start with seven stages, each with one owner and one output: intake, brief, production, review, approval, publishing, reporting. Skipping a stage creates bottlenecks later.

ul: Intake: capture every request in one form
Brief: write a one-page brief with goal, audience, format, deadline
Production: assign a producer who owns the timeline
Review: collect feedback in a single tool, not email threads
Approval: one named approver per asset type
Publishing: push to CMS or social scheduler from the same board
Reporting: track cycle time, revision rounds, on-time rate

sections.h2: What tool stack keeps a tiny team aligned?

blocks.p: Pick one work management tool, one brief repository, one publishing destination, and one reporting source. Adding more tools before you have volume creates fragmentation.

sections.h2: How do you prevent approval bottlenecks?

blocks.p: Name one approver per asset type and set a hard SLA. If the approver misses the window, the asset moves forward with a logged exception.

ol: List every asset type your startup produces
Assign a single approver for each type
Set a maximum review window in hours
Automate reminders at half the window and at expiry
Log exceptions in the work management board for retro review

sections.h2: When should you hire a dedicated creative operations person?

blocks.p: Hire when the founder or marketing lead spends more than ten hours a week chasing status, rewriting briefs, or fixing broken handoffs. Before that, a producer can own the process part-time.

ul: Cycle time exceeds ten working days for standard assets
Revision rounds average more than three per piece
On-time publishing rate drops below eighty percent
Team cannot answer 'where is this project?' in thirty seconds

sections.h2: What metrics prove the system works?

blocks.p: Track four core metrics monthly: cycle time from approved brief to publish, revision rounds per asset, on-time publishing rate, and capacity use per producer. Improving any one without worsening the others signals a healthy system.

ul: Cycle time: target five to ten working days for long-form
Revision rounds: target two or fewer
Capacity use: target seventy percent planned, thirty percent buffer

faq.q: Can a startup run creative operations without a dedicated tool?
faq.a: A shared spreadsheet works for the first five people, but it breaks when parallel projects exceed three. Move to a board-based tool as soon as two people wait on the same approver.

faq.q: How do you handle urgent requests that skip the intake form?
faq.a: Create an 'urgent' lane with a separate SLA. Require a one-line justification, the same approver, and a retroactive brief within twenty-four hours so reporting stays accurate.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to cut revision rounds?
faq.a: Enforce a complete brief before production starts. A brief checklist — goal, audience, format, deadline, brand assets, legal constraints — eliminates the most common rework causes.

faq.q: Should creative operations own the brand guidelines?
faq.a: Creative operations enforces guidelines; brand or design owns the content. Ops builds the checklist that forces every asset to pass a brand review gate before publishing.

faq.q: How do you scale the system when the team doubles?
faq.a: Split the producer role into intake coordinator and production manager. Keep one work management board, add a second review gate for high-risk assets, and introduce a monthly ops retro.
